title: Gravitational fields
source: Questions and terms copied unchanged from the site's bank, except where marked for IB Diploma Physics (status of the source: ai-reviewed-reverified-gate-verified-2026-09-29-awaiting-human-signoff). Terms and clues: D.1#c07 bank term, clue written for the game from the bank's definition; D.1#c01 bank term, clue written for the game from the bank's definition; D.1#c02 bank term, clue written for the game from the bank's definition; D.1#c03 bank term, clue written for the game from the bank's definition. Questions: D.1#q01, D.1#q04, D.1#q06, D.1#q07, D.1#q10, D.1#q02, D.1#q05, D.1#q08, D.1#q11, D.1#q03, D.1#q09, D.1#q12, D.1#q13, D.1#q15, D.1#q17, D.1#q18, D.1#q20.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Point mass
items.clue: An idealised body whose size and shape play no part.

items.label: Kepler's first law
items.clue: Each planet moves in an ellipse with the Sun at one focus.

items.label: Kepler's second law
items.clue: The line from a planet to the Sun sweeps out equal areas in equal times.

items.label: Kepler's third law
items.clue: The square of the orbital period is proportional to the cube of the mean distance from the Sun.

questions.stem: Kepler's third law describes the orbits of the planets around the Sun. Taking each orbit as a circle of radius r with time period T, which statement expresses the law?

options.text: T/r has the same value for every planet that orbits the Sun.
T has the same value for every planet, whatever its distance.
T²/r³ has the same value for every planet that orbits the Sun.
T²/r³ has one value for all orbiting bodies, whatever they orbit.

questions.explanation: This is Kepler's third law, T² ∝ r³. For circular orbits it follows from GMm/r² = m(2π/T)²r, which gives T²/r³ = 4π²/GM, the same for every planet because M is the Sun's mass.

questions.stem: The Earth exerts a gravitational force of 2.0 × 10²⁰ N on the Moon. The mass of the Moon is about 1.2% of the mass of the Earth. Which statement about the gravitational force that the Moon exerts on the Earth is correct?

options.text: It is 2.0 × 10²⁰ N, and it pulls the Earth towards the Moon.
It is about 1.2% of 2.0 × 10²⁰ N, as the Moon has far less mass.
It is zero, as a small body cannot attract a much larger one.
It is zero, as the Moon has no air and so has no gravity.

questions.explanation: The two forces are a Newton's third law pair: equal in size, opposite in direction. F = Gm₁m₂/r² contains the product of both masses, so the same value applies to each body. The force on the Earth points towards the Moon.

questions.stem: A planet is a sphere of uniform density. Why can it be treated as a point mass at its centre when calculating the gravitational force on a satellite orbiting it?

options.text: A satellite is usually far away compared with the planet's radius, so the planet looks like a point.
The satellite's mass is tiny compared with the planet's, so the planet's size is irrelevant.
All of the planet's mass is concentrated at its centre, where its gravity comes from.
At any point outside a uniform sphere, its field is that of a point mass at its centre.

questions.stem: Which statement defines the gravitational field strength g at a point?

options.text: The gravitational force acting on any object placed at that point, in newtons.
The gravitational force per unit mass on a small point mass placed at that point.
The acceleration of free fall at that point, which is 9.8 m s⁻² at every point.
The force per unit mass on a small point mass, directed away from the mass producing the field.

questions.explanation: This is the definition in the guide: g = F/m for a small test mass, one small enough not to disturb the field. The unit is N kg⁻¹, equivalent to m s⁻².

questions.stem: A student sketches the gravitational field lines around an isolated planet that is a uniform sphere. Which description of a correct sketch is right?

options.text: Straight radial lines pointing inwards to the planet's centre, closer together near its surface.
Straight radial lines pointing outwards from the planet's centre, closer together near it.
Parallel lines all pointing 'down' in one direction, equally spaced at all distances.
Curved lines that leave the planet near one pole and re-enter it near the other.

questions.stem: A comet moves around the Sun in a highly elliptical orbit. Which statement about the comet agrees with Kepler's laws?

options.text: It moves at the same speed at every point of its orbit.
It moves fastest when it is furthest from the Sun.
The Sun is at the centre of its elliptical orbit.
It moves fastest when it is nearest the Sun.

questions.explanation: Kepler's second law: the line from the Sun to the comet sweeps out equal areas in equal times. Near the Sun the swept triangle is short, so the comet must cover a longer arc in the same time: it is fastest at its closest approach and slowest at its furthest point.

questions.stem: A satellite of mass 1200 kg orbits the Earth at a height of 600 km above the surface. The Earth has mass 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg and radius 6370 km. Take G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻². What is the gravitational force that the Earth exerts on the satellite?
questions.explanation: r is measured from the Earth's centre: r = 6370 km + 600 km = 6970 km = 6.97 × 10⁶ m. F = GMm/r² = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 5.97 × 10²⁴ × 1200 / (6.97 × 10⁶)² = 9.84 × 10³ N.

questions.stem: At the surface of the Earth, g = 9.8 N kg⁻¹. Planet X has the same mass as the Earth but half its radius. Both may be treated as uniform spheres. What is the gravitational field strength at the surface of planet X?

options.text: 39.2 N kg⁻¹
19.6 N kg⁻¹
9.80 N kg⁻¹
4.90 N kg⁻¹

questions.explanation: g = GM/R². With the same M and half the R, g increases by a factor 1/(0.5)² = 4: 4 × 9.8 = 39.2 N kg⁻¹.

questions.stem: Close to the surface of a planet, over a region a few kilometres across, the gravitational field is drawn as parallel, equally spaced field lines pointing vertically downwards. What does this pattern show about the field in that region?

options.text: Any object released or thrown in the region moves along one of the field lines.
The field acts only along the lines drawn, with no field in the gaps between them.
The field strength has the same size and direction at every point in the region.
A heavier object placed in the region experiences a larger field strength.

questions.explanation: Parallel lines show the same direction everywhere, and equal spacing shows the same strength everywhere: a uniform field. This is the assumed uniform field close to the surface of a planet.

questions.stem: Io and Europa are moons of Jupiter, and their orbits may be taken as circular. Io has an orbital radius of 4.22 × 10⁸ m and a time period of 1.77 days. Europa has an orbital radius of 6.71 × 10⁸ m. What is the time period of Europa?

options.text: 2.81 days
3.55 days
1.77 days
4.48 days

questions.explanation: By Kepler's third law T² ∝ r³ for moons of the same planet, so T_E = T_I × (r_E/r_I)^(3/2) = 1.77 × (6.71/4.22)^(3/2) = 1.77 × 2.005 = 3.55 days.

questions.stem: The Earth (mass 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg) and the Moon (mass 7.35 × 10²² kg) are 3.84 × 10⁸ m apart, centre to centre. At one point on the line joining their centres, the resultant gravitational field strength is zero. How far is this point from the centre of the Earth?
questions.explanation: Set GM_E/x² = GM_M/(d − x)²: x/(d − x) = √(M_E/M_M) = √81.2 = 9.01, so x = 9.01d/10.01 = 3.46 × 10⁸ m, about 90% of the way to the Moon.

questions.stem: The gravitational potential energy E_p of a system is the work done to assemble the system from infinite separation of its components. Why is E_p of an Earth–satellite system negative?

options.text: The minus sign shows that the potential energy is directed towards the centre of the Earth.
Positive work is needed to bring them together, so the minus sign is only a convention.
Energy has been used up in bringing them together, leaving the system with an energy deficit.
The bodies attract, so the work done to bring them together from infinity is negative.

questions.stem: A satellite of mass 500 kg is moved from a circular orbit of radius 6.80 × 10⁶ m to a circular orbit of radius 2.04 × 10⁷ m around the Earth, of mass 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg. Take G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻². The gravitational field strength at the Earth's surface is 9.8 N kg⁻¹. What is the change in the gravitational potential energy of the Earth–satellite system?
Which statement about the gravitational potential V_g at a point outside a planet is correct?

options.text: It is the gravitational potential energy of any mass at the point, measured in joules.
It is the work done per unit mass to bring a small mass from infinity to the point, and is negative.
It is zero at the planet's surface and increases with height above it, as mgh does.
It is the gravitational force per unit mass on a small mass at the point, directed inwards.

questions.explanation: This is the guide's definition, V_g = −GM/r. It is zero at infinity and negative at every finite distance, because the planet attracts the mass as it is brought in. Unit: J kg⁻¹.

questions.stem: Two equipotential surfaces around the Earth are 1.00 × 10⁵ m apart along a radial line. The inner surface has V_g = −6.251 × 10⁷ J kg⁻¹ and the outer surface has V_g = −6.155 × 10⁷ J kg⁻¹. Taking r as increasing outwards from the Earth's centre, what is the average gravitational field strength g between the two surfaces?

options.text: +9.6 N kg⁻¹ (directed away from the Earth)
−9.8 N kg⁻¹ (directed towards the Earth’s centre)
0 N kg⁻¹ (each surface is an equipotential)
−9.6 N kg⁻¹ (directed towards the Earth)

questions.explanation: g = −ΔV_g/Δr = −(−6.155 × 10⁷ − (−6.251 × 10⁷))/1.00 × 10⁵ = −(9.6 × 10⁵)/(1.00 × 10⁵) = −9.6 N kg⁻¹. The minus sign means the field points towards decreasing r, towards the Earth.

questions.stem: An external force moves a 3.0 kg mass at constant speed from a point where the gravitational potential is −3.2 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹ to a point where it is −1.1 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹. What is the work done on the mass by the external force?
questions.explanation: W = mΔV_g = m(V_final − V_initial) = 3.0 × (−1.1 × 10⁶ − (−3.2 × 10⁶)) = 3.0 × 2.1 × 10⁶ = +6.3 × 10⁶ J. The mass moves to a higher (less negative) potential, so positive work is done.

questions.stem: Equipotential surfaces are drawn around an isolated planet that is a uniform sphere, at equal intervals of gravitational potential. Which description is correct?

options.text: Concentric spheres, equally spaced at all distances from the planet's centre.
Concentric spheres, further apart the further they are from the planet.
Radial straight lines that point inwards towards the planet's centre.
Concentric spheres, on each of which the gravitational field strength is zero.

questions.explanation: V_g = −GM/r depends only on r, so equipotentials are spheres centred on the planet. Equal steps in V_g need larger steps in r further out, where the field is weaker, so the spacing increases with distance.
